newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia restructures monopolies, sees boom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia restructures monopolies, sees boom.

text.p: Russian officials, promising an investment boom this year, announced plans on Wednesday to transform two of their biggest natural monopolies in a further move towards an open market economy.
The plans could help clear the way to additional payments from the International Monetary Fund, which is likely to make release of 1997 funds conditional on industrial restructuring.
But neither natural gas monopoly Gazprom nor utility RAO UES will be completely broken up.

Analysts said plans to offer 25 percent of telecoms giant Svyazinvest to portfolio investors could prove unpopular because the unwieldy company lacked strategic direction and was likely to underperform regional telecom firms and the market.

The Russian share market, by some measurements the strongest-performing emerging market of 1996, has risen to new highs this year, shrugging off political uncertainty triggered by President Boris Yeltsin's absence with pneumonia.
Yeltsin returned to the Kremlin on Wednesday to meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

"Russia has become more or less mainstream," said Christopher Granville, chief economist at United City Bank. "I think investors are not really worried any more about chronic political destabilisation."
Foreign direct investment in Russia is still low by international standards but Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said investment could rise to $5 bilion this year.
"We had foreign investment of about $2.5-3.0 billion last year, without state Treasury bills. This year we can expect between $4 and $5 billion," he told a news conference.

Yasin also said the government planned to split off the distribution unit of national electricity company RAO UES's from the rest of the firm, allowing individual power plants to offer supplies to consumers aT competitive prices.
The domestic operations of Gazprom would also change, but there were no plans to alter its international operations.
"The most important thing for industry is to decrease utility costs and decrease debt," Yasin said. "We expect fulfillment of the programme will result in higher household (utility) prices."
Corporate debt and wage arrears are among Russia's biggest economic problems and a senior parliamentarian warned on Wednesday that government debt was getting out of hand.
"More and more is being spent to service debt and less and less is available for spending," said Mikhail Zadornov, head of the lower house of parliament's budget committee.
He said domestic debt would rise to 690 trillion roubles ($123 billion) by the end of this year.
Yasin also outlined elements of Russia's economic plans for the next three years and said the government hoped for five percent growth by the year 2000.
Gross domestic product contracted by six percent last year. Industrial output, which has halved since Russia launched its market reforms in January 1992, contracted by five percent.
